s: Wine Spectator exclusive, 1 Jul 2015, on the $315M Meiomi sale to Constellation (he was 33); Forbes profile of Copper Cane, 19 Jun 2025
m: Meiomi sold for $315M cash in Aug 2015 at a reported 24x earnings multiple, roughly $210M net of California and federal capital gains, plus Copper Cane at about 1M cases across Elouan, Belle Glos and Quilt valued near 2x revenue
did: Created Meiomi in 2006 as a Pinot Noir blended across three coastal counties, grew it past 700,000 cases and sold the brand alone - no vineyards, no winery - to Constellation for $315 million in 2015, then built Copper Cane around Elouan, Belle Glos and Quilt.
why: Meiomi was a label and a grower book, not an estate. Because no capital was tied up in land, the thing Constellation bought was pure margin on contracted fruit, which is why a brand with no winery fetched 24 times earnings.
obst: Oregon growers and regulators forced Copper Cane to strip Willamette Valley appellation language off Elouan in 2018 because the fruit was trucked to California to be made, costing him the brand story on his largest post-Meiomi launch.
turn: Selling the brand in 2015 rather than the business - he kept the winemaking team and the grower contracts, so Copper Cane relaunched at scale inside a year.

s: The Drinks Business and Wine-Searcher on the 2016 E&J Gallo purchase of Orin Swift at a reported $300M; Wine Spectator on the $40M Prisoner sale to Huneeus in 2010; birth date 2 Jan 1973
m: Reported $300M Gallo purchase of Orin Swift in 2016 plus $40M for The Prisoner in 2010 and the 2018 Locations sale, roughly $230M net of California and federal capital gains, plus Department 66 in Roussillon and Napa and Santa Barbara vineyard holdings
did: Founded Orin Swift in 1998 with two tons of borrowed Zinfandel, created The Prisoner with its Goya etching label and sold it to Huneeus for $40 million in 2010, then sold the entire Orin Swift brand to E&J Gallo in 2016 for a reported $300 million.
why: Napa sold varietal and appellation; he sold label art and narrative. A red blend with no stated pedigree cannot be price-compared to a Rutherford Cabernet, so he charged $40 for open-market fruit and kept the spread instead of buying land.
obst: For a decade he owned no vineyards and no winery, buying fruit and renting crush space, so every vintage was a fresh negotiation and one grower defection could end a brand; he then had to watch two labels he invented go to buyers.
turn: The 2010 sale of The Prisoner for $40 million, which proved a Napa red blend with no estate behind it was a tradable asset and set the template he repeated at ten times the price six years later.

s: Variety, Napa Valley Register and Arnold & Porter deal announcement on the $315M Treasury Wine Estates purchase of Frank Family Vineyards, closed 13 Dec 2021 (he was 78)
m: $315M all-cash sale in Dec 2021 of a winery he and Leslie Frank controlled, about $210M net of California and federal capital gains, plus the retained Winston Hill and Lewis vineyards in Rutherford and Napa and prior Disney-era equity
did: Ran Walt Disney Studios as president through the animation revival and chaired Disney Television, then in 1992 bought Hanns Kornell's bankrupt Larkmead property in Calistoga and built Frank Family into a 100,000-case Chardonnay and Cabernet house sold to Treasury for $315 million.
why: He treated the tasting room as a hospitality business with a managed club list years before Napa took direct-to-consumer seriously, so Treasury was buying a named customer file and a Chardonnay brand at volume rather than acreage it could have bought cheaper.
obst: The site was a wrecked sparkling-wine facility from a bankruptcy and he entered Napa as a Hollywood outsider with no growing background; the 2020 Glass Fire burned to the edge of Napa's Calistoga vineyards the year before he sold.
turn: Abandoning sparkling wine in the late 1990s and making Carneros Chardonnay the flagship, which became the volume engine and the specific asset Treasury wanted.

s: Wine Spectator, Apr 2016, on Constellation buying The Prisoner Wine Company from Huneeus Vintners for $285M; Wine Spectator, May 2019, giving his age as 53 at his guilty plea
m: His share of the Huneeus family holding: The Prisoner bought for $40M in 2010 and sold for $285M in 2016, roughly $165M net of tax split with his father, plus Quintessa, a 280-acre Rutherford estate, and the Faust and Illumination brands
did: Co-founded Huneeus Vintners with his father in 2005, bought The Prisoner from Dave Phinney for $40 million in 2010, more than doubled its production and sold it to Constellation for $285 million in 2016, while running the family's 280-acre Quintessa estate in Rutherford.
why: The arbitrage worked because the brand's creator refused to scale it. Huneeus already had the grower relationships and bulk-fruit access to double volume without touching the label, converting a cult wine into a distribution asset inside six years.
obst: He pleaded guilty in the 2019 Varsity Blues case for paying $50,000 to have a proctor correct his daughter's SAT answers, served five months in federal prison, and had to hold the family company and its distributor relationships together through it.
turn: The April 2016 sale of The Prisoner for $285 million, which turned a $40 million bet into the capital base that now carries Quintessa and the rest of the portfolio.

s: Beckstoffer Vineyards and Wikipedia acreage disclosures - 1,072 acres in Napa, 1,138 in Mendocino, over 1,100 in Lake County - against 2023-24 Napa vineyard parcel transaction data
m: 1,072 Napa acres at a conservative $300k per acre is $322M; roughly 2,240 Mendocino and Lake County acres at $30-35k adds about $73M; call it $395M of land less mortgage debt and generational transfers to his children
did: Bought Heublein's Vinifera Development Corporation and its 1,200 Napa and Mendocino acres in 1973, then assembled six heritage vineyards including To Kalon, Dr. Crane and Georges III, about 3,300 acres across three counties, and became the largest non-winery vineyard owner in Napa.
why: In 1976 he replaced tonnage pricing with a formula tying the price per ton to about 100 times the retail bottle price of the finished wine. That one contract term moved the margin on Napa Cabernet from the winery to the grower and never moved back.
obst: Phylloxera destroyed most of Napa's AxR1 rootstock between 1987 and 1994 and he had to replant hundreds of acres at his own cost with no crop in the interim; earlier he had to buy the vineyard subsidiary out from under a corporate parent exiting the business.
turn: Buying the 89-acre core of To Kalon in Oakville in 1993 and then selling its fruit by named block to small producers, which created the vineyard-designate market that Napa land is now priced against.

s: Contemporaneous reporting and Wikipedia on the 1 Aug 2007 agreement to sell Stag's Leap Wine Cellars for $185M to UST Inc and Marchese Piero Antinori; born 22 Oct 1928
m: $185M in 2007, roughly $140M after federal and California capital gains, less about $55M of disclosed giving including a $50M matching grant to St. John's College in 2018, plus the retained Arcadia Vineyard in Coombsville and nineteen years of investment return
did: Left a University of Chicago political-philosophy career, bought a 44-acre Napa prune orchard in 1970, and made the 1973 Cabernet that beat Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion at the 1976 Paris tasting, then sold Stag's Leap Wine Cellars for $185 million in 2007.
why: The Paris tasting was blind and judged by French palates, so the result could not be written off as American boosterism. One afternoon moved Napa Cabernet from discount substitute to competing luxury good, and he held the label that proved it.
obst: He had no winemaking training, no family in the trade and had bought fruit-orchard ground nobody believed was Cabernet land; even after 1976 the winery was tiny and expansion had to be funded from cash flow against far better capitalised Napa rivals.
turn: The 24 May 1976 Paris tasting, where his 1973 Cabernet placed first, which repriced his fruit, his land and ultimately the company he sold three decades later.

s: Morning Star Company disclosures via Wikipedia (Oct 2023) and his Free To Choose Network board biography: sole owner, revenue above $1B, about 40% of California processing tomatoes, BA 1972
m: Sole ownership of Morning Star: revenue above $1B at a commodity tomato-paste EBITDA margin near 6% valued at 7x gives roughly $420M enterprise value, less seasonal and term debt, plus his own tomato acreage and the trucking arm
did: Started in 1970 hauling tomatoes in one truck, built the world's largest tomato processor at Woodland and Los Banos handling about 5 million tons a year, and runs it with no managers and no titles - each of roughly 550 permanent staff negotiates a written agreement with peers annually.
why: Bulk tomato paste is won on cost per ton. Self-management deleted an entire supervisory layer and pushed capital-spend decisions down to the people running the evaporators, so the largest processor is also among the lowest cost - a compounding advantage in a commodity.
obst: Processing tomatoes has a single hundred-day harvest window with prices fixed before planting, so a Central Valley water allocation cut can strand a plant for a season; he also had to hold the no-manager structure intact through every growth phase that normally forces hierarchy.
turn: Building his own processing plant in 1990 rather than continuing to broker and haul other people's tomatoes, which moved him from trucking margins onto processing margins on the same tonnage.

s: SEC Schedule 13D filed 30 Aug 2004 and 13D/A of 22 Dec 2004 confirming the $56.50 per share cash merger with Constellation; Robert Mondavi Corp DEF 14A of Oct 2003 listing his age as 60
m: 1,534,088 Class A-equivalent shares at the $56.50 cash merger price is about $87M gross in Dec 2004, less option strikes, plus 425k Class B shares in his wife's and children's trusts; roughly $72M net of tax compounded 22 years, plus Folio Fine Wine Partners and the Animo vineyard on Atlas Peak
did: Co-founded the Robert Mondavi Winery with his father in 1966 and ran it as chairman, cashed 1.5 million shares at $56.50 in Constellation's 2004 buyout of the family company, then started over at 61 building Folio Fine Wine Partners as an importer and producer and planting Animo on Atlas Peak.
why: The 1993 Robert Mondavi IPO put a public price on Napa family equity for the first time, and the dual-class structure let the family keep voting control while marking the stake to market. That structure is what converted acreage into cash when Constellation bid in 2004.
obst: He was removed from the chairmanship in 2004 as the Woodbridge value tier dragged earnings and activist holders pressed, and the board then sold the company his father founded out from under three generations of the family.
turn: Constellation's November 2004 all-cash offer at $56.50 a share, which ended family ownership and handed him the liquidity he used to build a second business.

s: SEC Schedule 13D of 30 Aug 2004 and 13D/A of 22 Dec 2004 pricing Robert Mondavi shares at $56.50 cash; Robert Mondavi Corp DEF 14A of Oct 2003 listing his age as 52
m: 895,350 shares at the $56.50 cash merger price is about $51M gross in 2004 less option strikes, plus 338,058 Class B shares in his children's trusts; the larger asset is Continuum Estate, 172 acres on Pritchard Hill making roughly 10,000 cases at top Napa pricing
did: Was winegrower and vice chairman of the Robert Mondavi Corporation from 1974, and after Constellation bought the family company at $56.50 a share in 2004 founded Continuum Estate with his sister and father, buying 172 acres on Pritchard Hill and making a single Cabernet blend.
why: Continuum launched under a family name that already had global distribution, so it skipped the decade of brand-building a new Napa estate normally needs. One wine off hillside fruit means no value tier to defend and nothing to discount in a soft year.
obst: He was the winemaker publicly blamed for the quality drift that preceded the 2004 sale and had to rebuild credibility from unplanted Pritchard Hill ground, with no winery of his own for the first several vintages of Continuum.
turn: Buying the Pritchard Hill property in 2008 and moving Continuum entirely onto estate fruit, which gave the brand a defensible site instead of a purchased-grape blend.
